questions.question: Describe the composition and four-layer structure of the atmosphere, and explain the principle that the air is heated from below, naming the four heat-transfer processes.
questions.expected_answer: The atmosphere is about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen, with argon just under 1 per cent and the trace gases doing outsized work: carbon dioxide at about 0.04 per cent and water vapour at up to about 4 per cent trap outgoing heat, while ozone absorbs incoming ultraviolet. The troposphere holds nearly all weather and cools with height at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre up to the tropopause; the stratosphere warms with height because the ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet there; the mesosphere cools again and holds the coldest point, where meteors burn; the thermosphere heats steeply as thin air absorbs raw solar energy. Heating works from below: incoming shortwave insolation mostly passes through the air, with roughly half reaching and warming the surface, and the surface then radiates longwave terrestrial energy that greenhouse gases intercept — which is why temperature falls with altitude, and why Drakensberg mornings can be frosty while Durban is warm. Heat is distributed by radiation (energy as waves), conduction (contact between ground and the air touching it), convection (warmed air rising vertically) and advection (heat carried sideways by wind). The natural greenhouse effect keeps the planet livable — around minus 18 degrees without it — while the enhanced greenhouse effect from added carbon dioxide and methane drives warming.

questions.question: Trace the chain from water vapour to rain, and distinguish the three rainfall types with a South African example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Vapour enters the air by evaporation from sea, dams and soil and by transpiration from plants. Relative humidity expresses the vapour present as a percentage of the maximum air at that temperature could carry; because warm air carries more vapour, cooling air raises relative humidity without adding water until the dew point, where the air is saturated at 100 per cent. Further cooling forces condensation onto nuclei of dust, salt and smoke — dew, frost, mist and fog at ground level, cloud aloft. Cirrus clouds are high icy streaks, cumulus are heaped convection towers that can grow into the thunder-bearing cumulonimbus, and stratus are grey drizzling sheets. All significant rain requires rising air, because rising air cools and cooling wrings out the water, and there are exactly three lifts. Convectional rain: strong surface heating drives air upward — the Free State summer afternoon, with Bloemfontein under a hail-bearing storm by four o'clock. Orographic rain: moist air forced up a mountain barrier rains on the windward slope and leaves a rain shadow beyond — Indian Ocean air watering the forests above George on the Outeniquas while Oudtshoorn sits dry behind the crest. Frontal rain: a warm air mass is levered up over cold along a front — the winter cold fronts from the Southern Ocean that give Cape Town and the south-western Cape their wet winters, while the interior receives summer convectional rain.

questions.question: Summarise plate tectonics from evidence to landforms, and then work through the core mapwork skills: gradient from map measurements, contour interpretation, and the station model with a passing cold front.
questions.expected_answer: Wegener argued continental drift from the jigsaw fit of continents, fossils such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris on both sides of the Atlantic, matching rock sequences, and glacial scars in now-warm lands; mantle convection currents later supplied the engine, carrying lithospheric plates over the asthenosphere. Divergent boundaries build mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys; convergent boundaries subduct ocean floor to feed volcanic chains like the Andes and island arcs like Japan, or crumple continent against continent into the Himalayas; transform boundaries store strain released as earthquakes, as on the San Andreas. Slow compression folds rock into anticlines and synclines — the Cape Fold ranges, about 300 million years old — while snapping produces normal and reverse faults, with a dropped graben like the East African Rift and a raised horst as block mountain. An earthquake's focus is the underground rupture point, the epicentre the surface point above it; magnitude measures energy with one instrument-read number, Mercalli intensity the varying observed effects. In mapwork, on a 1:50 000 sheet 2 centimetres represent 1 kilometre and the contour interval is 20 metres; contours never cross, crowding means steep ground, and valley Vs point upstream. Gradient: heights 1 220 and 1 060 metres give a rise of 160 metres; 4.8 centimetres of map distance converts to 2 400 metres; 2 400 divided by 160 is 15, so the gradient is 1 in 15 — one metre climbed per fifteen travelled. The station model shows cloud cover in eighths, a wind shaft from the direction the wind comes with feathers in knots, temperature upper left and dew point lower left — converging values signalling rain. Ahead of a cold front the Cape is warm with northerly wind and falling pressure; behind it the wind veers south-west, temperature drops, pressure climbs and showers clear.
